summary: Specifies which set of RFCs make up version 3 of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP), and responds to the IESG Note attached to RFCs 2251 through 2256. It was replaced by RFC 4510.

plainLanguage.summary:
LDAPv3 was published as eight separate documents in two batches. The first six carried a warning that they should not be deployed because they required secure authentication for updates but did not say how to do it.

This RFC names the nine documents that together make up LDAPv3, and closes that warning by including the authentication document it had asked for.

questions: what is the ldap technical specification
what was the iesg note on ldapv3
which rfc covers ldap authentication methods
subtitle: The document that names the set of RFCs that make up LDAPv3 and closes the IESG note on authentication.

tldr.problem: LDAPv3 had been published as eight separate RFCs in two batches, and the first six carried an IESG note discouraging deployment because they mandated no workable authentication for update access.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3377 lists the nine RFCs that together constitute LDAPv3 and formally addresses the note by including RFC 2829, the authentication document the note had asked for.
tldr.outcome: The note is withdrawn by inclusion, and other documents are asked to cite RFC 3377 rather than the informal name LDAPv3. RFC 3377 was later obsoleted by RFC 4510.

today: RFC 3377 was a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 4510, which is the document to read for the LDAPv3 specification set today.

sections.title: Why LDAPv3 Needed Its Own Specification
sections.content:
The specification for the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol version 3 nominally comprised eight RFCs which were issued in two distinct subsets at separate times: RFCs 2251 through 2256 first, then RFCs 2829 and 2830 following later.

RFCs 2251 through 2256 do not mandate the implementation of any satisfactory authentication mechanisms, and so they were published with an IESG Note discouraging implementation and deployment of LDAPv3 clients or servers implementing update functionality until a Proposed Standard for mandatory authentication in LDAPv3 was published. RFC 2829 was subsequently published in answer to that note.

The stated purpose of RFC 3377 is to explicitly specify the set of RFCs comprising LDAPv3, and to formally address the IESG Note through the explicit inclusion of RFC 2829.
sections.plainLanguage: LDAPv3 was published in pieces, and the first pieces carried a warning label saying they should not be used yet.

sections.title: The RFCs That Make Up LDAPv3
sections.content:
The RFC states that LDAPv3 is specified by a set of nine RFCs, and lists them. RFC 2251 is the specification of the LDAP on-the-wire protocol. RFC 2252 gives the attribute syntax definitions. RFC 2253 gives the UTF-8 string representation of distinguished names. RFC 2254 gives the string representation of LDAP search filters. RFC 2255 gives the LDAP URL format. RFC 2256 is a summary of the X.500(96) user schema for use with LDAPv3. RFC 2829 covers authentication methods for LDAP. RFC 2830 is the LDAPv3 extension for Transport Layer Security. The ninth is RFC 3377 itself.

The RFC then makes a naming point. The term LDAPv3 is often used informally to refer to the protocol specified by the above set of RFCs, or subsets of them. The LDAPv3 protocol suite, as defined here, should be formally identified in other documents by a normative reference to RFC 3377.
sections.plainLanguage: The suite is nine documents: the protocol itself, the syntaxes, the name and filter formats, the URL format, the user schema, authentication, transport security, and this document that names the set.

sections.title: Addressing the IESG Note
sections.content:
The IESG approved publishing RFCs 2251 through 2256 with an attendant IESG Note included in each document. The Note begins with the statement that the document describes a directory access protocol providing both read and update access, that update access requires secure authentication, and that the document does not mandate the implementation of any satisfactory authentication mechanisms.

The Note ends with a statement that implementors are hereby discouraged from deploying LDAPv3 clients or servers which implement the update functionality, until a Proposed Standard for mandatory authentication in LDAPv3 has been approved and published as an RFC.

RFC 2829 is expressly the Proposed Standard for mandatory authentication in LDAPv3 called for in the Note. Because it is included in the set that constitutes LDAPv3, the IESG Note in RFCs 2251, 2252, 2253, 2254, 2255 and 2256 is addressed.
sections.plainLanguage: The warning on the first six documents asked for a mandatory authentication standard to be written before anyone deployed the update part of LDAP. That standard was RFC 2829, and listing it here closes the warning.

sections.title: Where the Security Detail Lives
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section of RFC 3377 says that the document does not directly discuss security, although the context of the IESG Note is security related, as is the manner in which it is addressed. It asks readers to refer to the referenced documents, especially RFC 2829, RFC 2251 and RFC 2830, for further information concerning LDAPv3 security.

The document also carries a standard intellectual property notice. The IETF takes no position on the validity or scope of any intellectual property or other rights that might be claimed to pertain to the implementation or use of the technology described, and it invites anyone who believes such rights may cover technology needed to practice the standard to bring that to the attention of the IETF Executive Director.
sections.plainLanguage: This document has almost nothing to say about security itself. It points to the authentication document, the protocol document and the transport security document for the detail.
